subject: chemistry
question_text: Write a short note on enthalpies for different types of reactions.

verification.note: Unit 6 Thermodynamics is sourced from the Sri Chaitanya Junior Fastrack chemistry section (book pp.73-75), which prints the question, its star rank and a model answer covering formation, fusion, vapourisation, sublimation and combustion. Only ONE source book is held for chemistry — the TSBIE Basic Learning Material in hand covers physics only — so the two-book union check is PENDING a second chemistry source. This chapter has NO Long Answer section in the book, so no 8-mark form is invented. The 1+1+1+1 mark split over five definitions is a CLAIM until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it. DISCREPANCY: the book defines heat of combustion as burning at constant volume; enthalpy is a constant-pressure quantity (heat at constant volume measures ΔU), so this card writes constant pressure and records the book's version. AI chemistry check 2026-08-25. The constant-pressure correction stands, and every value was recomputed or checked (−393.5, +6.0, +40.8, −890.3 kJ mol⁻¹). Added to the why channel: C(s) means graphite (the reference form) and the definition given is the STANDARD enthalpy of formation; and the sublimation sum rule holds only at ONE temperature, so the melting-point and boiling-point water values above must not simply be added. No marked line changed.

steps.label: Enthalpy of formation
lines: Enthalpy of formation: the enthalpy change
when one mole of a compound forms from its

lines.text: C(s) + O₂(g) → CO₂(g)  ΔH = −393.5 kJ mol⁻¹

steps.why: Formation enthalpies give every compound one reference number, from which reaction enthalpies can be calculated by Hess law. Elements in their standard states means the reference form of each element: the C(s) written here is graphite, and −393.5 kJ mol⁻¹ is the graphite value, not the diamond value. Because the standard-state condition is part of the definition, the quantity defined here is the STANDARD enthalpy of formation, ΔfH°.
common_mistakes: Leaving out one mole of the compound.
Leaving out from its elements — formation is always from elements, not from other compounds.
steps.memory_tip: Formation: elements combine into one mole of compound.
steps.margin_note: One line of definition plus one balanced equation each.

steps.label: Fusion and vapourisation
lines: Enthalpy of fusion: the enthalpy change
when one mole of a solid melts at its
change when one mole of a liquid becomes
steps.why: Melting and boiling are physical changes rather than reactions, but each still has a definite heat per mole at constant pressure. Both absorb heat, so both values are positive.
common_mistakes: Writing negative signs — fusion and vapourisation both absorb heat.
Swapping the two values: boiling needs far more heat than melting.
steps.memory_tip: Water: 6 to melt, about 41 to boil — boiling costs about seven times more heat.
steps.margin_note: Both definitions with the water values.

steps.label: Sublimation
lines: change when one mole of a solid changes
directly into its vapour, without melting.
By Hess law it equals the sum of the other
steps.why: Solid to vapour directly, and solid to liquid to vapour, connect the same two states — so by Hess law their enthalpies must be equal. All three values must be taken at the SAME temperature. The two water values in the previous step are not: 6.0 kJ mol⁻¹ is quoted at the melting point and 40.8 kJ mol⁻¹ at the boiling point, so adding those two does not give the enthalpy of sublimation of ice, which is about 51 kJ mol⁻¹ at 273 K.
common_mistakes: Defining sublimation with decomposition — the substance must reach the vapour unchanged.
Writing ΔH(sub) = ΔH(vap) − ΔH(fus). The two are added.

Adding the 6.0 and 40.8 kJ mol⁻¹ water values from the previous step to get a sublimation enthalpy. Those two are quoted at different temperatures; the sum rule needs all three values at one temperature.
steps.memory_tip: Sublimation skips the liquid stage but its enthalpy still counts both steps: fusion plus vapourisation.
steps.margin_note: The Hess relation is the detail that earns this mark.

when one mole of a substance burns
completely in excess oxygen at constant

lines.text: Combustion is always exothermic: ΔH is negative

steps.why: Enthalpy is the heat at constant pressure, so the definition must say constant pressure. The source book prints at constant volume — heat at constant volume measures ΔU, not ΔH — so this card corrects it and records the book's version.
common_mistakes: Writing at constant volume in the definition — the enthalpy of combustion is a constant-pressure quantity.
Giving a positive ΔH for combustion.
steps.memory_tip: Complete burning, excess oxygen, constant pressure, negative ΔH — four checks for one definition.
steps.margin_note: Box the sign rule: every combustion value is negative.

insider_note: Five definitions in four marks: one tight line each plus one balanced equation with a real value is what a full-mark answer looks like.
